title: To the ends of the earth (Acts 1:6–8)
hookLine: you shall receive power and be witnesses

cards: Some stories get a sequel. Luke's does. His Gospel finishes with Jesus blessing the disciples and being carried up into heaven.

Then he writes a second volume, addressed to the same reader, someone called Theophilus, and opens it by saying, in my first book I told you what Jesus began to do and to teach. Began. Everything so far was the beginning.
This is that second book, the Acts of the Apostles. It opens on a hill outside Jerusalem, with the disciples asking the wrong question.

teach.h: WILL YOU RESTORE THE KINGDOM NOW?
teach.b: For forty days after the resurrection, Luke says, Jesus has been appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God. Now they ask: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?
It's an understandable question. They want to know when, and they want it to look like what they expected. Jesus doesn't argue.
The times, he says, aren't theirs to know.

teach.h: JERUSALEM TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: Then he gives them something else, in the Douay-Rheims: "But you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost coming upon you, and you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth."
Then he's lifted up and a cloud takes him out of their sight. That one sentence is a map of the whole book.
Acts starts in Jerusalem, moves out into Judea and Samaria, and ends with Paul preaching in Rome, the empire's capital. The word to hold is witness.
In Greek it's martys. A witness, in a courtroom, is someone who says what they saw. Not an expert, not a salesman, just someone who was there.
In time, Christians used the same word for those who died rather than deny what they'd seen: martyr. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness. But here Jesus doesn't tell them to die.
He tells them who they'll be: people whose lives tell what they've seen.
Not you shall do witnessing, but you shall be witnesses.
It's a description, not a task list.

how: Catholics hear Acts 1:1–11 on the Solemnity of the Ascension, forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many places), and Acts is read at weekday and Sunday Masses through the Easter season.

o: someone who says what they saw, and was there
a preacher trained to win over a crowd
an expert called in to explain the facts

games.q: the second book — tap the pairs.

s: the disciples asked when the kingdom would be restored to Israel
Acts 1:6; Jesus says the times aren't theirs to know.
Acts 1:8 maps the book: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the ends of the earth
the story moves outward and ends in Rome.
the word martyr originally meant someone who dies
martys first meant a witness, someone who saw.

games.q: you're with the risen Jesus on a hill outside Jerusalem. you ask when the kingdom will be restored. what does he give you instead of a date?
o: the promise of power to be his witnesses.
games.why: you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost, and you shall be witnesses, even to the uttermost part of the earth.

practice: Picture yourself from the outside, the way a coworker or a neighbor or a kid sees you on an ordinary day, and ask what they'd say you care about just from watching: not from what you say, but from what you do.
No judging, just noticing. If you pray, hold the line, you shall be witnesses unto me; if you don't, just hold the picture.

wordCard.voice: Witness. In Greek, martys: someone who tells what they saw, and later, someone who gave their life for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: witnesses (Acts 1:8), from martys, the root of martyr.

carryVoice: Your line: you shall be witnesses. Someone who was there, saying what they saw. That's day five hundred thirty-four.
